drug_class: Integrase Strand Transfer Inhibitor (INSTI) — a type of antiretroviral (HIV) medicine
purpose: Dolutegravir is used to treat HIV (Human Immunodeficiency Virus) in adults and children. It is always used together with other HIV medicines as part of a combination treatment plan. It helps control HIV so you can live a healthier life, though it does not cure HIV.
how_it_works: HIV needs to copy itself inside your body's cells to survive and multiply. Dolutegravir blocks a key tool the virus uses — called integrase — which the virus needs to insert its genetic material into your cells. By blocking this step, the medicine stops HIV from making more copies of itself, keeping the virus at very low levels in your blood.
common_side_effects: Trouble sleeping or vivid dreams, headache, tiredness, nausea or upset stomach, dizziness, and mood changes. Most of these tend to be mild and may improve as your body gets used to the medicine.
warnings: Tell your doctor if you are pregnant or planning to become pregnant — there may be a small risk of birth defects if taken very early in pregnancy, so your doctor will weigh the benefits and risks with you. This medicine can affect your liver, so report yellowing of skin or eyes, dark urine, or stomach pain right away. It can also cause mood changes or depression — contact your doctor if you feel unusually sad or have thoughts of self-harm. Some people experience a reaction called IRIS (immune reconstitution syndrome) when starting HIV treatment, where the immune system reacts to hidden infections. Always take it as prescribed and never stop without talking to your doctor first.
typical_dosing: For most adults, the usual dose is one 50 mg tablet taken by mouth once a day, with or without food. Some patients — such as those on certain other medicines — may need to take it twice a day. Your doctor will decide the right dose for you. Take it at the same time each day to help you remember.
